prompt: Deliveries with a coupon took 9.8 minutes longer, and 17 of the 29 coupons went to the far neighbourhood. What best explains the gap?

choices.text: Couriers ride slower with coupon orders
choices.why: Nothing in the data points to that; distance explains the gap.

choices.text: Distance drives both coupons and duration
choices.why: Right. Far customers got more coupons, and far deliveries take longer.

choices.text: Chance, since p is small
choices.why: A small p makes chance unlikely, not likely.

choices.text: Coupon orders carry more items
choices.why: Items barely move delivery times, and the coupons followed distance.

prompt: How does this lesson test whether distance is behind the coupon gap?

choices.text: By running a larger survey of customers
choices.why: More of the same data would show the same confounded gap.

choices.text: By asking couriers why they were slow
choices.why: Opinions are not a comparison that holds distance fixed.

choices.text: By removing deliveries over 50 minutes
choices.why: That throws away data without holding distance fixed.

choices.text: By comparing within each neighbourhood
choices.why: Right. Holding the confounder roughly fixed, the gap nearly vanishes.

prompt: Neighbourhoods with more couriers on shift have more late deliveries. Which explanation does this lesson find most likely?
hint: Who decides how many couriers go where?

choices.text: Late areas are sent extra couriers
choices.why: Right. The dispatcher responds to lateness, so the arrow runs backwards.

choices.text: Extra couriers get in each other's way
choices.why: Possible, but it ignores how couriers are assigned.

choices.text: The correlation is a coincidence
choices.why: There is a clear mechanism; chance is not needed.

choices.text: Late deliveries make couriers quit
choices.why: That would mean fewer couriers, not more.

prompt: Why is "first A happened, then B" not enough to show that A caused B?

choices.text: Because time order is irrelevant to causes
choices.why: It matters: a cause must come first. It is just not sufficient.

choices.text: Because B might have come first after all
choices.why: The question assumes the order is known.

choices.text: A third cause could produce that order
choices.why: Right. The rooster crows before sunrise and causes nothing.

choices.text: Because only experiments have a time order
choices.why: Observational data has time order too.

prompt: Two monthly series that drift over time correlate at −0.79, but their month-to-month changes correlate at 0.07. What does that suggest?
hint: What do two drifting lines always share?

choices.text: The changes hide a strong negative link
choices.why: Changes remove the trend, and nothing is left.

choices.text: One series causes the other with a delay
choices.why: Nothing points to a delayed effect.

choices.text: The correlation comes from the two trends
choices.why: Right. Any two drifting series correlate; their changes show no link.

choices.text: Thirty-six months is too short for r
choices.why: The levels gave a large r on the same 36 months.

prompt: Analysts saw bullet holes clustered on the wings of returning bombers. Why did Abraham Wald advise armouring the places with few holes?
hint: Which planes were not in the data?

choices.text: Planes hit in those places did not return
choices.why: Right. The data held only survivors, so few holes marked the fatal spots.

choices.text: Wings were already strong enough
choices.why: Strength was not his argument; missing planes were.

choices.text: Holes in the wings were measurement errors
choices.why: The holes were real.

choices.text: Gunners aimed mostly at the wings
choices.why: Even if so, the missing planes are the key.

prompt: Motorbikes made 88 on-time deliveries out of 94 near ones. What percentage is that? Give one decimal place.
Bicycles were on time for 241 of 280 near deliveries and 52 of 76 far ones. What is their overall on-time percentage? Give one decimal place.
hint: Add the on-time counts and the totals first.

prompt: Motorbikes beat bicycles near and far, yet lose overall. Why?
hint: How are each vehicle's trips split between near and far?

choices.text: The percentages were computed wrongly
choices.why: Every rate is correct; the mix of trips differs.

choices.text: Bicycles are faster in heavy traffic
choices.why: Then bicycles would win within the groups.

choices.text: The samples are too small to compare
choices.why: Hundreds of deliveries per vehicle is plenty.

choices.text: Motorbikes take most far trips
choices.why: Right. Their total is mostly a far rate, where everyone is late more.

prompt: When is the combined table, not the split one, the fair comparison?
hint: Think of blood pressure measured after the treatment.

choices.text: When the subgroups are small
choices.why: Size does not settle it; the causal story does.

choices.text: When the split variable is an effect
choices.why: Right. Splitting by something the treatment changes hides its effect.

choices.text: When the totals favour the new option
choices.why: Choosing the view by its answer is p-hacking.

choices.text: Whenever the split table reverses
choices.why: A reversal alone does not say which view is right.

prompt: What does randomly assigning coupons achieve that adjusting for distance cannot?

choices.text: It makes the sample larger
choices.why: The number of deliveries can be the same either way.

choices.text: It balances unmeasured factors too
choices.why: Right. Adjustment handles only what was measured.

choices.text: It guarantees a significant result
choices.why: It guarantees a fair comparison, not a small p.

choices.text: It removes the need for a control group
choices.why: The customers who get no coupon are the control.

prompt: Which belong in a well-run randomised trial? Choose all that apply.
hint: Which option brings back human choice?

choices.text: A control group at the same time
choices.why: Yes: anything else that changes affects both groups.

choices.text: The outcome chosen before the data
choices.why: Yes: lesson 14's defence against p-hacking.

choices.text: Staff choosing who seems suitable
choices.why: That lets a confounder pick the groups again.

choices.text: Blinding, where possible
choices.why: Yes: expectations cannot shift the outcome.

prompt: Why could the routing trial of lesson 13 not prove that the new system caused any change?

choices.text: Its p-value was too large
choices.why: Even a small p would not have fixed the design.

choices.text: Twenty-five deliveries is too few to test
choices.why: Small samples cost power; the design problem is separate.

choices.text: A one-sided test cannot show causes
choices.why: The sidedness is not the problem.

choices.text: It had no group at the same time
choices.why: Right. A change in traffic would be confounded with the system.

prompt: Which of Bradford Hill's points does "heavier smokers had higher rates" illustrate?
hint: More of one, more of the other.

choices.text: Dose and response
choices.why: Right. More of the cause goes with more of the effect.

choices.text: Consistency
choices.why: Consistency is the same finding in different studies.

choices.text: Time order
choices.why: That is about the cause coming first.

choices.text: Experiment
choices.why: That is about removing the cause.

prompt: Which sentence describes the coupon data without claiming a cause?

choices.text: Coupons lengthen deliveries
choices.why: "Lengthen" is a causal verb.

choices.text: Coupons lead to slower couriers
choices.why: "Lead to" claims a cause.

choices.text: Coupon orders had longer deliveries
choices.why: Right. It reports what happened and nothing more.

choices.text: Coupons drive up delivery times
choices.why: "Drive up" smuggles in a cause.
